doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Joining the Erskine Hawkins band
summary: Leaving Don Redman at the Zanzibar, he joined Hawkins, whom he knew from Pensacola, and stayed twelve years in an unintegrated band.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Maybe I’d love to. Can you tell me how it came about that you joined Erskine Hawkins?
Oh, how I joined Erskine’s? Well it’s easy. Erskine’s band stayed with us when we had our hotel, or whatever you called it—

In Pensacola. Some people have a different word for it, you know what I mean? Because there was always a lot of females around, a lot of booze and everything. And they stayed with us. So when I came to New York they’d already, they were on top. They had played the Savoy Ballroom, and I was with, maybe you haven’t heard of this band, one of the great bands of our time, I was with the Don Redman Band on Broadway at the Cafe Zanzibar. And we closed one night, closed on a Sunday. And they had heard of me. They knew me when I was a kid. So I came — I went out to get a paper, and when I came back my little wife and daughter, she said, “Erskine Hawkins’ manager wanted to talk to you.” I said, “About what?” She said, “He would like for you to join his band.” I said, “Ah, naah, that’s not me.” So she says, “Well you’re not working,” and she brought it home to me she says, “You’re not working, why don’t you take your horn and get the bus and go on.” At that particular time bus fare, 8th Avenue bus fare was a nickel. So I got on the bus at 113th Street, got off at 142nd Street, and heard this great band playing. And I went up and that particular night I think the draft board came up and took three. They took the late and great Mr. Renauld Jones, they took Jimmy Harris, took about five others. So that left the trumpet section empty. Then when I told Erskine, I laid it on the line, I said I don’t play lead trumpet, I’m a trumpet soloist. So he said, “Ah we knew you when you was a kid, we know who you are.” So I played. Then maybe you’ve heard of one of our

great trumpet players of our time, his name is Dud Bascomb, he was the one who made that trumpet solo in “Tuxedo Junction” with the Erskine Hawkins Band. So I stayed for a week, and the Savoy Ballroom, the money was very — the scale I think was only like $39 or something like that. So I stayed, and the guys began to like me. And as you know, Erskine’s band never integrated. We never had — we never — and that was one of the things that really hurt me. We never had any people of color in that band, but I stayed with them twelve years. But I’m glad I did, because I will say that I got a chance to record. Erskine always had a trumpet soloist, and I will say that if you came by my house I could say that I recorded the most trumpet solos with another trumpet player, another great trumpet player’s band, than anyone. And I don’t regret it at all. That’s one of the ways. I knew them from the south. They liked southern musicians. I don’t think we’ve ever had a southerner in the band, the only one, the southern was maybe Kelly Martin, our drummer, that was with Erroll Garner later on in life. But I stayed with him a long time, and he paid me very well, Erskine did. I did all right with that band.
